beats.headline: One class serving 3 business actors will break production.
beats.subline: When finance rules, email templates, and SQL queries share a file, small edits cause cascading bugs.
beats.narration: When finance updates tax rules, why does email formatting break? Mixing multiple business actors inside a single class creates fragile code that fails when independent teams request changes.

beats.title: God Class vs. Isolated Actor Boundaries

top.label: Monolithic OrderService
points: Cannot unit test without live DB

bottom.label: Focused Collaborators
points: Each class answers to one actor

beats.narration: In monolithic services, tax calculation, HTML rendering, and raw SQL execution sit together. Splitting them into distinct collaborators allows each business concern to evolve without risking side effects across unrelated modules.

beats.title: Extensible Strategy with OCP

steps.explanation: Defines an explicit extension seam so new payment providers require zero edits to existing dispatch logic.
PaymentEngine handles registration and execution without growing massive if-else conditional chains.

beats.narration: The Open Closed Principle means open for extension, closed for modification. By dispatching through a registry map, adding Apple Pay only requires creating a new strategy class rather than editing existing core engine code.

beats.title: Open Polymorphism vs. Sealed Exhaustiveness
beats.subtitle: Choosing the right abstraction model in modern Java

nodes.label: Open Interfaces
nodes.detail: Plugin architectures with unknown future implementations

nodes.label: Sealed Hierarchies
nodes.detail: Fixed domain states checked at compile-time by compiler

nodes.label: Pattern Switch
nodes.detail: Exhaustive branch validation without fallback default clauses

beats.narration: Use open interfaces when third party plugins will expand your system over time. But for fixed domain states like payment outcomes, Java 21 sealed hierarchies offer compiler checked exhaustiveness across switch expressions.

beats.title: SRP & OCP Fundamentals Locked
takeaways: SRP = isolated responsibilities per business actor
OCP = extend behavior without altering core code
Prefer sealed interfaces when variant sets are fixed
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Liskov Substitution & the silent Square-Rectangle bug →
beats.narration: That covers SRP and OCP. In Part 2, we dive into Liskov Substitution and reveal why standard subclassing breaks behavioral runtime expectations.

beats.headline: Subclasses can pass compilation yet shatter runtime logic.
beats.subline: The Java compiler checks method signatures, but it cannot enforce behavioral promises.
beats.narration: Your subclass can compile with zero warnings while completely breaking caller assumptions. Subtype substitution requires strict adherence to behavioral contracts, not just matching method signatures.

beats.title: The Classic Square-Rectangle Trap

steps.explanation: Rectangle promises callers that mutating width leaves height unaffected.
Square mutates both dimensions together, breaking callers expecting area of 20 after setting 5x4.

beats.narration: Rectangle promises independent width and height modification. Square overrides setWidth to alter height simultaneously. When passed to code expecting standard rectangle behavior, calculated areas produce wrong numbers at runtime.

beats.title: Broken Subtype vs. Immutable Sealed Model

top.label: Throwing Mutator Subclass

bottom.label: Sealed Record Hierarchy
points: Subtypes share clean contract without mutation

beats.narration: Subclasses throwing UnsupportedOperationException violate behavioral expectation rules. Replace invalid inheritance hierarchies with composition or shared immutable records implementing focused interfaces.

beats.title: The 4 Behavioral Rules of LSP
beats.subtitle: Guarantees required for safe subtype substitution

nodes.label: Preconditions
nodes.detail: Subtypes cannot reject valid inputs accepted by base types

nodes.label: Postconditions
nodes.detail: Subtypes must deliver state promises made by supertypes

nodes.label: Invariants
nodes.detail: Supertype internal state rules must remain fully preserved

nodes.label: No Unexpected Exceptions
nodes.detail: Subtypes must not throw unexpected runtime failures

beats.narration: Four rules protect subtype substitution: never strengthen preconditions, never weaken postconditions, preserve supertype state invariants, and avoid throwing unannounced runtime exceptions.

beats.title: Subtype Contracts Validated
takeaways: Subclasses must honor supertype behavioral promises
Avoid overriding methods just to throw exceptions
Favor composition and immutable records over mutable subclassing
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Segregating fat interfaces & Dependency Inversion →
beats.narration: Now you understand LSP constraints. In Part 3, we fix wide fat interfaces using ISP and decouple domain core policies using Dependency Inversion.

beats.headline: Fat interfaces force classes to write useless stub methods.
beats.subline: When interfaces combine unrelated duties, implementers end up coupled to code they never use.
beats.narration: Why should an automated CI bot implement human timesheet methods? Interface Segregation keeps contracts small and client focused, while Dependency Inversion turns package dependencies inward toward core logic.

beats.title: Bloated Interface vs. Focused Role Interfaces

top.label: Fat Monolithic Interface
points: Forces bots to implement human methods
Changes for human workflows touch bot code

bottom.label: Segregated Role Contracts
points: Classes implement only what they support
Clients depend strictly on needed operations

beats.narration: Grouping unrelated responsibilities into giant interfaces forces implementers to throw exceptions or supply empty stubs. Splitting them into role interfaces ensures classes adopt only the capabilities they genuinely support.

beats.title: Dependency Inversion in Architecture
beats.subtitle: Inverting compile-time arrows toward core domain logic

nodes.label: Domain Core
nodes.detail: High-level business rules owning the repository interface port

nodes.label: AccountRepository
nodes.detail: Pure abstraction seam residing inside core business package

beats.narration: Dependency Inversion flips compile time dependencies. High level domain logic owns the port interface, while low level infrastructure adapters like PostgreSQL implement that interface from outer layers.

beats.title: Domain Policy Decoupled from Infrastructure

steps.explanation: Owned by domain core with zero imports of JDBC, Hibernate, or Spring framework classes.
Executes domain logic and relies on abstraction for state updates.

beats.narration: Notice how TransferFundsUseCase stays completely clean. It has zero dependencies on databases or frameworks. It operates strictly through the domain-owned AccountRepository abstraction.

beats.title: ISP & DIP Cleanly Integrated
takeaways: ISP = small role interfaces tailored to client needs
DIP = core business rules own abstractions
Decouple domain policy from database implementation details

parts.partTitle: Pragmatic SOLID, Modern Java & Practical Trade-Offs

beats.headline: Creating Service and ServiceImpl everywhere is an anti-pattern.
beats.subline: Blindly applying design abstractions creates unnecessary tax without giving flexibility.
beats.narration: Creating matching interfaces for single concrete classes is a classic Java over-abstraction trap. SOLID principles are design heuristics to manage real change, not dogma to apply blindly.

beats.title: Dogmatic Over-Abstraction vs. Pragmatic Concrete First

top.label: 1:1 Interface Wrapper Tax
points: Doubles file count with zero runtime benefits
Forces IDE navigation jumps to find code

bottom.label: Concrete First, Refactor Later
points: Extract interfaces when multiple implementations emerge
Keep code readable until friction demands abstractions

beats.narration: Do not write one-to-one interfaces for every service class before you actually need a second implementation or test seam. Start concrete and extract interfaces when friction appears.

beats.title: Modern OCP: Sealed Interfaces + Pattern Switch

steps.explanation: Restricts implementation variants explicitly within the domain layer.
Pattern switch requires handling all cases, eliminating runtime missing-branch bugs.

beats.narration: Modern Java gives us powerful options beyond traditional polymorphism. Sealed interfaces paired with switch pattern matching deliver full compiler checked exhaustiveness across closed sets of business outcomes.

beats.title: Testing DIP In-Memory Repositories
beats.caption: Fast unit tests using plain Java test double implementations

lines.text: # Run unit tests using lightweight in-memory storage adapters
BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 850ms (0 external DB calls required)

beats.narration: Applying Dependency Inversion pays instant testing dividends. By substituting fast in-memory repository adapters into unit tests, test suites execute in milliseconds without launching database containers.

beats.title: SOLID Mastery Unlocked!
takeaways: SOLID principles manage code change, not file counts
Use sealed pattern matching for fixed domain variants
Start concrete and extract interfaces when seams emerge
